title: Day 63 · Week 9, Day 0 — Body: the first choreography — the embryo has been moving for a week, the one-second bend from the spinal cord, the general movement that means the brain has joined in, the hiccup on a three-second clock, and why she'll feel none of it until Day 112
summary: Week 9 opens the last full week of the embryonic period. Your baby is at Carnegie stage 20 (post-fertilization day 49; 18–22 mm): fingers separated by programmed cell death, toes forming, an elbow, a pigmented eye with the first eyelid fold, an ear canal, the liver bulging, the trunk straightening and the head lifting, a vascular network under the scalp; stages 21–23 follow by Day 70 (hands meeting, the tail going, head half the body, 'external genital primordium developing'). The arm nerves are already in adult arrangement (Shinohara 1990, 8 embryos). The heart peaks at about 170 bpm at 9–10 weeks (Doubilet & Benson 1995; Papaioannou 2010, 4,698 pregnancies) and a normal early heartbeat carries 91.4% first-trimester success (Doubilet & Guo 2024). The main event: spontaneous movement, from the Groningen films (de Vries, Visser & Prechtl 1982, 1985, 1988; 11–12 women scanned an hour a week from 7 weeks) and the IVF series (Lüchinger 2008; 18 embryos). First movements at 7.5 weeks — a one-second sideways bend of head or rump, generated by spinal cord and brainstem; arms and legs joining by 8.5 weeks; general movements from 8–9 weeks (whole-body, varying in speed, force and direction — the signature of supraspinal modulation, i.e. the brain joining in; sideways bends fall at 9 weeks, p=0.01, general movements rise, p=0.006); startles; hiccups from about 9 weeks at a preferred interval of 1–3 seconds; isolated arm movements about one a second; then head movements, hand–face contact, breathing movements from 10 weeks (rhythm shifting from one per 2–3 s to under 1 s by 19 weeks), jaw opening, stretch, yawn, sucking and swallowing by 12.5 weeks; all 16 patterns present in every fetus by 15 weeks. Between 8 and 19 weeks the longest stillness was 13 minutes; no male–female difference in any pattern, but consistent individual differences in activity. Unlike Hooker's filmed reflex (Day 57), these need no stimulus. Why she feels nothing: a 20 mm body in a fist-sized uterus below the pubic bone; quickening at 16–22 weeks (Day 112–154; Day 153 coming). The nine-week scan: CRL curves (Robinson; Hadlock 1992, 416 women, ±8%; Pexsters 2010, 3,710 pregnancies) agree at 9 weeks; ACOG CO 700 redating only if >7 days apart; movement is reliably visible now — ask to watch for twenty seconds; and sex cannot be read yet (genital tubercle indifferent; tubercle-angle technique at 11–14 weeks; Day 69 Myths coming). The cochlear duct completes its 2.5 turns by the end of the embryonic period; hearing itself is Day 161.
action: Ten minutes tonight, and one request at the scan. One: on the Dates page of the Day 61 file, add three lines — 'movement began: about Day 52, unfelt'; 'quickening window: Day 112 to Day 154'; and beside the scan date, the Day 56 rule, 'CRL replaces the period date only if more than seven days apart'. Two: at this week's scan, after the measurement, ask the sonographer: 'Can we watch for twenty seconds and see it move?' If it does, write 'movement seen, Day ___' on the back of the Day 42 card under the heart rate; if it doesn't, write '13 min' beside it, the longest it would have stayed still. Three: if the scan has already happened and nobody looked, nothing is lost — the next one shows more, and Day 153 is where movement starts to matter.
